bromides and aromatic anhydrides as dual electrophiles. This protocol enables eficient assembly of tetrasubstituted allenyl ketones
with high chemo- and regioselectivity. Mechanistic insights reveal the radical relay process involving the synergistic interactions of
nickel and zinc. The allenyl ketone products serve as modular building blocks, particularly for constructing fully carbon-substituted
furans via Au-catalyzed cycloisomerization with selective 1,2-aryl migration, enhancing the synthetic practicality.

over, these methods frequently require stoichiometric oxidants
or moisture-sensitive organometallic reagents yet remain

pot strategy that can simultaneously introduce both the allenyl
and ketocarbonyl units from simple starting materials is
urgently needed.
Recent years have witnessed significant advances in radical-
mediated 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes,<sup>8</sup>
enabling
eficient access to multisubstituted allenes bearing cyano,
aryl,<sup>10</sup> alkynyl,<sup>11</sup> and halo groups.<sup>12</sup> In contrast, the catalytic
synthesis of allenyl ketones via radical 1,4-difunctionalization
of 1,3-enynes remains underdeveloped (Scheme 1b). Notable
research by Du, Huang and Li demonstrated NHC-catalyzed
1,4-alkylacylation through allenyl-ketyl radical cross-cou-
pling,
albeit limited to activated radical precursors like alkyl
halides, redox ester, ring-strained oxime esters and Togni
reagent due to NHC’s constrained reducing power. Subse-
quent work by Zhang and Wang achieved 1,4-sulfonylacylation
and fluoroalkylative acylation with sulfinates and acyl fluorides
via NHC/photoredox dual catalysis.<sup>14</sup> Concurrently, Kong’s
group achieved 1,4-alkylacylation via synergistic photocata-
lyzed hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and nickel catalysis,<sup>15</sup>
though requiring large excesses of saturated hydrocarbons as
radical precursors. Most recently, Wu and Guo independently
established palladium- and nickel-catalyzed four-component
1,4-alkylcarbonylation using the CO insertion strategy.<sup>16</sup>
Despite these remarkable advances, it is still desirable to
explore modular strategies enabling the eficient assembly of
structurally diverse, fully substituted allenyl ketones from
bench-stable feedstocks.
The nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling paradigm has driven
transformative advances in alkene/alkyne difunctionalization,
with recent extensions to 1,3-enynes demonstrating excep-
tional site selectivity. Notably, Rueping’s and our independent
studies established electrochemical and photochemical 1,4-
alkylarylation of 1,3-enynes through a synergistic merger of
nonactivated alkyl bromides as bench-stable precursors.
Following these seminal works, subsequent contributions
from Hong, He and Wei further advanced this paradigm.

smooth transformation to aford products 4a-4g with
comparable eficiencies (63−68% yield). However, upon
replacement of the ester group, the reaction led to a decreased
yield (4h), accompanied by the formation of a certain amount
of hydroalkylation byproducts. Further examination of steric
influences demonstrated that meta- or ortho-substituted
substrates with methoxy or methyl groups (4i-4j) maintained
satisfactory reactivity, indicating remarkable tolerance toward
steric hindrance in this catalytic protocol. Notably, the
extension of the C-2 aryl group to 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl
(4k) led to a diminished yield. When heterocyclic systems,
such as 1,3-benzodioxolyl and thiophene, were applied, the
desired products were obtained with moderate yields (4l-4m).
Studies on C-4 substituents showed efective compatibility
with both linear alkyl chains (4n, 4o) and branched alkyl
groups (4p, 4q), delivering the target products in acceptable
yields. However, the reaction proved intolerant to extreme
steric bulk, as evidenced by complete inhibition with tert-butyl
or trimethylsilyl substituents, ascribed to the inaccessibility of
the metal catalytic center.

A series of control experiments were conducted to clarify the

studies with 1,1-diphenylethylene selectively captured tert-
butyl radicals (8b, 25% GC yield), while control experiments
with benzoic anhydride revealed no detectable benzoyl radical
adducts (8c/8c′), establishing the involvement of alkyl radical
species (Scheme 6b). Notably, tert-butyl radical generation
persisted without LiBr (8b, 30% GC yield), excluding LiBr’s
participation in radical initiation. Removing the nickel catalyst
and ligand unexpectedly enhanced the formation of 8b (39%
GC yield), demonstrating that zinc-mediated reductive
cleavage of the C−Br bond serves as the predominant radical
source. However, we could not exclude the competent
reductive cleavage of tert-butyl bromide with a low-valence
nickel complex (Scheme 6c). Furthermore, the model reaction
employing 10 mol % Ni(COD) as a catalyst aforded product
4a with 42% isolated yield, whereas no product was observed
with stoichiometric Ni(COD) in the absence of zinc powder
(Scheme 6d). These observations indicate that Ni(0)
preferentially undergoes irreversible oxidative addition with
benzoic anhydride,<sup>21</sup> forming a thermodynamically stable
Ni(II)-benzoyl complex that deactivates alkyl bromide
activation, thereby interrupting the catalytic cycle.
Based on the above mechanistic evidence and precedent
literature,<sup>22</sup> a plausible catalytic cycle is proposed in Scheme
6e. Initiation involves Zn-mediated reduction, generating
active Ni(0) species A, which engages in oxidative addition
with benzoic anhydride 3 to form Ni(II)-acyl complex B.
Concurrently, tert-butyl bromide 2 undergoes single-electron
transfer (SET) mediated by zinc or low-valent nickel species,
liberating a tertiary alkyl radical that participates in
